blocks.body:
What should $(1/2)!$ mean? The factorial is defined by repeated multiplication, which only makes sense for whole numbers, yet formulas in probability, geometry and number theory keep producing $n!$ in places where $n$ wants to be a fraction or even a complex number. The gamma function is the standard answer: one function, given by an integral, that matches the factorial at the integers (shifted by one), obeys the same recursion everywhere, and extends to the whole complex plane apart from isolated poles.

In number theory the motivation is sharper: the Riemann zeta function satisfies a symmetric functional equation only after it is multiplied by a gamma factor, and the same holds for every $L$-function. Euler found the function in 1729, in letters to Christian Goldbach, while looking for a way to interpolate $n!$ between the integers.

blocks.title: An integral that produces factorials
blocks.body:
For an integer $n \ge 0$ put $I_n = \int_0^\infty x^n e^{-x}\,dx$. Clearly $I_0 = 1$. Integrating by parts with $u = x^n$ and $dv = e^{-x}\,dx$ gives $I_n = \bigl[-x^n e^{-x}\bigr]_0^\infty + n\int_0^\infty x^{n-1}e^{-x}\,dx = n I_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$, because the boundary term vanishes at both ends. Hence $I_n = n!$.

Nothing in the integral forces $n$ to be an integer. For complex $s$ and $x > 0$ define $x^{s-1} = e^{(s-1)\log x}$; then $|x^{s-1}| = x^{\sigma-1}$ where $\sigma = \operatorname{Re} s$. At the end $x = \infty$ the factor $e^{-x}$ beats every power of $x$, so that half of the [[improper-integrals|improper integral]] always converges. Near $x = 0$ we have $e^{-x} \approx 1$, so convergence there is the same as convergence of $\int_0^1 x^{\sigma-1}\,dx$, which happens exactly when $\sigma > 0$.

blocks.title: The gamma function
blocks.body:
For complex $s$ with $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$,
$$\Gamma(s) = \int_0^\infty x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx.$$
The integral converges absolutely in this half-plane, and it converges uniformly on every strip $a \le \operatorname{Re} s \le b$ with $0 < a < b$, so $\Gamma$ is holomorphic for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. By the calculation above, $\Gamma(n+1) = n!$ for every integer $n \ge 0$.

blocks.title: Functional equation of Γ
blocks.body:
For $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$,
$$\Gamma(s+1) = s\,\Gamma(s), \qquad \Gamma(1) = 1,$$
and consequently $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$ for every integer $n \ge 1$.

Integrate by parts on $[\varepsilon, R]$:
$$\int_\varepsilon^R x^{s}e^{-x}\,dx = \bigl[-x^s e^{-x}\bigr]_\varepsilon^R + s\int_\varepsilon^R x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx.$$
As $\varepsilon \to 0^+$ the term $\varepsilon^s e^{-\varepsilon}$ tends to $0$, because $|\varepsilon^s| = \varepsilon^{\operatorname{Re} s}$ and $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. As $R \to \infty$ the term $R^s e^{-R}$ tends to $0$. Taking both limits gives $\Gamma(s+1) = s\,\Gamma(s)$. Also $\Gamma(1) = \int_0^\infty e^{-x}\,dx = 1$, and induction gives $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)\Gamma(n-1) = \dots = (n-1)!\,\Gamma(1) = (n-1)!$.

blocks.title: Continuing to the left
blocks.body:
The integral only defines $\Gamma$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$, but the functional equation shows how to go further. Read backwards it says $\Gamma(s) = \Gamma(s+1)/s$. The right side makes sense for $\operatorname{Re} s > -1$, $s \ne 0$, and agrees with $\Gamma$ where both are defined. Repeating this $n$ times,
$$\Gamma(s) = \frac{\Gamma(s+n)}{s(s+1)\cdots(s+n-1)},$$
which defines a meromorphic function on $\operatorname{Re} s > -n$ whose only possible poles are at $0, -1, \dots, -(n-1)$. Different choices of $n$ agree where they overlap, so by the uniqueness of [[continuation|analytic continuation]] there is exactly one meromorphic function on $\mathbb C$ that equals the integral when $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. We keep calling it $\Gamma$.

A second construction makes the poles explicit and uses only [[series|power series]]. Split the integral at $x = 1$ and expand $e^{-x} = \sum_k (-1)^k x^k/k!$ on $[0,1]$; integrating term by term is allowed for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ because the series of absolute values converges. The result is
$$\Gamma(s) = \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^k}{k!\,(s+k)} + \int_1^\infty x^{s-1}e^{-x}\,dx.$$
The integral on the right converges for every complex $s$ and is an entire function of $s$. On any compact set avoiding $0, -1, -2, \dots$ the $k$-th term of the series is at most a constant times $1/k!$, so the series converges uniformly there and defines a meromorphic function. The right side is therefore the continuation of $\Gamma$, valid on all of $\mathbb C$.

blocks.title: Poles and residues
blocks.body:
$\Gamma$ is meromorphic on $\mathbb C$. Its only poles are simple poles at $s = 0, -1, -2, \dots$, and
$$\operatorname{Res}_{s=-k}\Gamma(s) = \frac{(-1)^k}{k!} \qquad (k = 0, 1, 2, \dots).$$

Use the series formula. Near $s = -k$ every term except the $k$-th is holomorphic, and so is the integral; the $k$-th term is $\frac{(-1)^k}{k!}\cdot\frac{1}{s+k}$. At points other than $0, -1, -2, \dots$ everything is holomorphic.

blocks.title: The value at 1/2 and the Beta integral
blocks.body:
Substituting $x = u^2$ in the definition gives $\Gamma(1/2) = \int_0^\infty x^{-1/2}e^{-x}\,dx = 2\int_0^\infty e^{-u^2}\,du = \sqrt\pi$, the Gaussian integral. The functional equation then gives $\Gamma(3/2) = \tfrac12\sqrt\pi$ and $\Gamma(5/2) = \tfrac34\sqrt\pi$, and going left, $\Gamma(-1/2) = \Gamma(1/2)/(-1/2) = -2\sqrt\pi$. So the answer to the opening question is $(1/2)! = \Gamma(3/2) = \sqrt\pi/2$.

Products of gamma values come from a double integral. For $\operatorname{Re} a > 0$ and $\operatorname{Re} b > 0$ the Beta integral is $B(a,b) = \int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt$.

blocks.title: Euler's Beta integral
blocks.body:
For $\operatorname{Re} a > 0$ and $\operatorname{Re} b > 0$,
$$B(a,b) = \int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt = \frac{\Gamma(a)\,\Gamma(b)}{\Gamma(a+b)}.$$

Write $\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b) = \int_0^\infty\!\int_0^\infty x^{a-1}y^{b-1}e^{-(x+y)}\,dx\,dy$. The double integral converges absolutely, so we may change variables and use Fubini's theorem. Put $x = ut$, $y = u(1-t)$ with $u > 0$ and $0 < t < 1$. This maps the strip $(0,\infty)\times(0,1)$ bijectively onto the open quadrant, with Jacobian determinant of absolute value $u$. Since $x^{a-1}y^{b-1} = u^{a+b-2}t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}$ and $x + y = u$,
$$\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b) = \int_0^\infty u^{a+b-1}e^{-u}\,du\int_0^1 t^{a-1}(1-t)^{b-1}\,dt = \Gamma(a+b)\,B(a,b).$$

blocks.title: Reflection formula
blocks.body:
For every $s \in \mathbb C \setminus \mathbb Z$,
$$\Gamma(s)\,\Gamma(1-s) = \frac{\pi}{\sin \pi s}.$$
In particular $\Gamma$ has no zeros, and $1/\Gamma$ is an entire function whose zeros are exactly $0, -1, -2, \dots$.

First let $0 < s < 1$. The Beta integral with $a = s$, $b = 1-s$ gives $\Gamma(s)\Gamma(1-s) = \Gamma(1)B(s, 1-s) = \int_0^1 t^{s-1}(1-t)^{-s}\,dt$. The substitution $t = u/(1+u)$, which maps $(0,\infty)$ onto $(0,1)$ with $dt = du/(1+u)^2$, turns this into
$$\int_0^\infty \frac{u^{s-1}}{1+u}\,du.$$
This integral equals $\pi/\sin\pi s$. That is a standard [[residues|residue]] calculation, which we only sketch: integrate $z^{s-1}/(1+z)$ around a keyhole contour that hugs the positive real axis, with $\arg z \in (0, 2\pi)$. The small and large circles contribute nothing in the limit because $0 < s < 1$, the two sides of the cut contribute $(1 - e^{2\pi i s})$ times the integral, and the residue at $z = -1$ is $e^{i\pi(s-1)} = -e^{i\pi s}$. So the integral is $-2\pi i\,e^{i\pi s}/(1 - e^{2\pi i s}) = \pi/\sin \pi s$.

Both sides of the reflection formula are meromorphic on $\mathbb C$ and they agree on the interval $(0,1)$, so by the identity theorem they agree everywhere. Since $\pi/\sin\pi s$ never vanishes, $\Gamma(s) \ne 0$ for $s \notin \mathbb Z$; at the positive integers $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)! \ne 0$, and the other integers are poles. So $\Gamma$ never vanishes. Finally $1/\Gamma(s) = \Gamma(1-s)\sin(\pi s)/\pi$: the poles of $\Gamma(1-s)$ at $s = 1, 2, \dots$ are cancelled by zeros of $\sin \pi s$, so $1/\Gamma$ is entire, and it vanishes exactly where $\Gamma$ has poles.

blocks.title: How big is Γ?
blocks.body:
For real $x \to \infty$, Stirling's formula says
$$\Gamma(x) \sim \sqrt{2\pi}\,x^{x-1/2}e^{-x},$$
which for $x = n+1$ is the familiar approximation of $n!$. More generally $\log\Gamma(s) = (s - \tfrac12)\log s - s + \tfrac12\log 2\pi + O(1/|s|)$ uniformly in any sector $|\arg s| \le \pi - \delta$. We omit the proof; it is in the references.

The consequence used most in number theory concerns vertical lines. For fixed real $\sigma$ and $|t| \to \infty$,
$$|\Gamma(\sigma + it)| \sim \sqrt{2\pi}\,|t|^{\sigma-1/2}e^{-\pi|t|/2}.$$
So $\Gamma$ decays exponentially as one moves up a vertical line. This is what makes contour integrals involving $\Gamma$ converge so well in the [[mellin|Mellin transform]], and it is how the gamma factor in the functional equation of $\zeta$ controls the size of $\zeta$ to the left of the critical strip.

blocks.title: Gaussian moments and negative half-integers
blocks.body: Evaluate $\int_0^\infty x^4 e^{-x^2}\,dx$ and $\Gamma(-3/2)$.
blocks.solution:
Substitute $x = \sqrt u$, so $dx = \tfrac12 u^{-1/2}\,du$. The integral becomes
$$\tfrac12\int_0^\infty u^{3/2}e^{-u}\,du = \tfrac12\Gamma(5/2) = \tfrac12\cdot\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac12\sqrt\pi = \frac{3\sqrt\pi}{8}.$$
The same substitution shows $\int_0^\infty x^m e^{-x^2}\,dx = \tfrac12\Gamma\bigl(\tfrac{m+1}{2}\bigr)$ for every real $m > -1$.

For $\Gamma(-3/2)$ run the recursion backwards: $\Gamma(-1/2) = \Gamma(1/2)/(-1/2) = -2\sqrt\pi$, and $\Gamma(-3/2) = \Gamma(-1/2)/(-3/2) = \tfrac43\sqrt\pi$. In general $\Gamma$ is positive on $(0,\infty)$, negative on $(-1,0)$, positive on $(-2,-1)$, and so on: the sign changes at each pole.

blocks.title: Trigonometric integrals from the Beta function
blocks.body: Compute $\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^6\theta\,d\theta$.
blocks.solution:
In the Beta integral substitute $t = \sin^2\theta$, so $1 - t = \cos^2\theta$ and $dt = 2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta$. This gives the general identity
$$\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^{2a-1}\theta\,\cos^{2b-1}\theta\,d\theta = \tfrac12 B(a,b) = \frac{\Gamma(a)\Gamma(b)}{2\,\Gamma(a+b)}.$$
For $\sin^6\theta$ take $2a - 1 = 6$ and $2b - 1 = 0$, that is $a = 7/2$, $b = 1/2$. Since $\Gamma(7/2) = \tfrac52\cdot\tfrac32\cdot\tfrac12\sqrt\pi = \tfrac{15}{8}\sqrt\pi$ and $\Gamma(4) = 6$,
$$\int_0^{\pi/2}\sin^6\theta\,d\theta = \frac{\tfrac{15}{8}\sqrt\pi\cdot\sqrt\pi}{2\cdot 6} = \frac{15\pi}{96} = \frac{5\pi}{32}.$$

blocks.title: Γ on vertical lines
blocks.body: Show that for real $t$, $|\Gamma(\tfrac12 + it)|^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{\cosh\pi t}$, and for real $t \ne 0$, $|\Gamma(it)|^2 = \dfrac{\pi}{t\sinh\pi t}$.
blocks.solution:
First, $\overline{\Gamma(s)} = \Gamma(\bar s)$. For $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$ this follows by conjugating the integrand, and it extends to all $s$ through the formula $\Gamma(s) = \Gamma(s+n)/(s(s+1)\cdots(s+n-1))$, whose right side has the same property.

So $|\Gamma(\tfrac12+it)|^2 = \Gamma(\tfrac12+it)\Gamma(\tfrac12-it)$. The reflection formula with $s = \tfrac12 + it$, so that $1 - s = \tfrac12 - it$, gives
$$\frac{\pi}{\sin(\tfrac\pi2 + i\pi t)} = \frac{\pi}{\cos(i\pi t)} = \frac{\pi}{\cosh \pi t}.$$
For the second formula, $|\Gamma(it)|^2 = \Gamma(it)\Gamma(-it)$, and the functional equation gives $\Gamma(1 - it) = -it\,\Gamma(-it)$. Hence
$$\Gamma(it)\Gamma(-it) = \frac{\Gamma(it)\Gamma(1-it)}{-it} = \frac{\pi}{-it\,\sin(i\pi t)} = \frac{\pi}{-it\cdot i\sinh\pi t} = \frac{\pi}{t\sinh \pi t}.$$
Both formulas show the decay $|\Gamma(\sigma+it)| \approx \sqrt{2\pi}\,|t|^{\sigma-1/2}e^{-\pi|t|/2}$ predicted by Stirling: for instance $\pi/\cosh \pi t \approx 2\pi e^{-\pi|t|}$.

blocks.title: Gauss's limit and Wallis's product
blocks.body:
Prove Gauss's formula $\Gamma(s) = \lim_{n\to\infty}\dfrac{n!\,n^s}{s(s+1)\cdots(s+n)}$ for real $s > 0$, and deduce Wallis's product
$$\frac{\pi}{2} = \prod_{k=1}^\infty\frac{(2k)^2}{(2k-1)(2k+1)}.$$
blocks.solution:
Let $g_n(s) = \int_0^n x^{s-1}(1 - x/n)^n\,dx$. Substituting $x = nu$ and using the Beta integral,
$$g_n(s) = n^s\int_0^1 u^{s-1}(1-u)^n\,du = n^s B(s, n+1) = \frac{n^s\,\Gamma(s)\,n!}{\Gamma(s+n+1)}.$$
By the functional equation $\Gamma(s+n+1) = (s+n)(s+n-1)\cdots s\,\Gamma(s)$, so $g_n(s) = \dfrac{n!\,n^s}{s(s+1)\cdots(s+n)}$.

On the other hand, for $0 \le x \le n$ we have $0 \le (1 - x/n)^n \le e^{-x}$, because $\log(1 - y) \le -y$, and $(1 - x/n)^n \to e^{-x}$ for each fixed $x$. By dominated convergence, with dominating function $x^{s-1}e^{-x}$, we get $g_n(s) \to \Gamma(s)$.

Now take $s = \tfrac12$. Then $s(s+1)\cdots(s+n) = \dfrac{1\cdot 3\cdots(2n+1)}{2^{n+1}}$, so
$$\frac{2^{n+1}\,n!\,\sqrt n}{1\cdot3\cdots(2n+1)} \to \sqrt\pi.$$
Square this and write $(2^n n!)^2 = \prod_{k=1}^n(2k)^2$ and $\bigl(1\cdot3\cdots(2n+1)\bigr)^2 = (2n+1)\prod_{k=1}^n(2k-1)(2k+1)$. The squared quantity becomes
$$\frac{4n}{2n+1}\prod_{k=1}^n\frac{(2k)^2}{(2k-1)(2k+1)} \to \pi.$$
Since $4n/(2n+1) \to 2$, the partial products of Wallis's product tend to $\pi/2$.

blocks.body:
- $\Gamma(n) = (n-1)!$, not $n!$. The shift by one is a historical convention (the letter $\Gamma$ is Legendre's notation); $\Gamma(n+1) = n!$ is the safe form to remember.
- The integral formula is valid only for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$. For $\operatorname{Re} s \le 0$ the integral diverges, and $\Gamma(s)$ means the continuation, computed for example by $\Gamma(s) = \Gamma(s+n)/(s(s+1)\cdots(s+n-1))$.
- Matching the factorial at the integers does not single out $\Gamma$: for any constant $c$, the function $\Gamma(s)(1 + c\sin 2\pi s)$ has the same integer values and the same recursion. On $(0,\infty)$ the Bohr–Mollerup theorem characterises $\Gamma$ as the only positive function $f$ with $f(1) = 1$, $f(x+1) = x f(x)$ and $\log f$ convex.
- $\Gamma$ never vanishes. The negative integers are poles of $\Gamma$ and zeros of $1/\Gamma$.
- Stirling's formula is an asymptotic statement about the ratio: $\Gamma(x)/(\sqrt{2\pi}\,x^{x-1/2}e^{-x}) \to 1$, while the difference grows without bound.

The [[mellin|Mellin transform]] is built on the integral that defines $\Gamma$: $\Gamma(s)$ is the Mellin transform of $e^{-x}$, and Mellin inversion gives $e^{-y} = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\Gamma(s)\,y^{-s}\,ds$ for $c > 0$, the starting point for smoothed sums over integers.

For the [[zeta|Riemann zeta function]], the substitution $x = \pi n^2 t$ in $\Gamma(s/2)$ turns $\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)n^{-s}$ into $\int_0^\infty e^{-\pi n^2 t}t^{s/2-1}\,dt$. Summing over $n$ connects $\zeta$ with the theta function of [[fourier-poisson|Poisson summation]], and the result is the symmetric [[functional-equation]] for $\pi^{-s/2}\Gamma(s/2)\zeta(s)$. The trivial zeros of $\zeta$ at $-2, -4, \dots$ are the poles of $\Gamma(s/2)$ seen from the other side.

Outside number theory, $\Gamma$ gives the volume $\pi^{n/2}/\Gamma(\tfrac n2 + 1)$ of the unit ball in $\mathbb R^n$, and the normalising constants of the gamma, chi-squared and Student distributions in [[distributions|probability]].

1. Show that $\Gamma(n + \tfrac12) = \dfrac{(2n)!}{4^n\,n!}\sqrt\pi$ for every integer $n \ge 0$.
2. Show that $B(a,b) = \displaystyle\int_0^\infty\frac{u^{a-1}}{(1+u)^{a+b}}\,du$ for $a, b > 0$.
3. Show that $\displaystyle\int_0^1(-\log x)^{s-1}\,dx = \Gamma(s)$ for $\operatorname{Re} s > 0$.
4. Check that the residues $(-1)^k/k!$ of $\Gamma$ at $s = -k$ are consistent with the reflection formula, by computing the residue of $\pi/(\sin(\pi s)\,\Gamma(1-s))$ at $s = -k$.
